past_actions.summary: Pull a list of the 20 clients who haven't called in over a year and send them a personal check-in email — something warm, not salesy. Reference their specific policy, ask how the car is treating them, mention that rates are moving around and I want to make sure they're still getting a good deal. Sign it Tom, not 'Tom Bradley, Licensed Agent.'
past_actions.emotional_state: A low-grade unease that I've gotten good at not looking at directly. On the surface: calm, professional, experienced. Underneath: a persistent background hum — like a refrigerator you stop hearing until it suddenly goes quiet, and then the silence is louder than the noise ever was. I'm not scared. I'm not ready to be scared yet. That's probably its own kind of problem.

past_actions.summary: Follow up personally by phone with the two clients whose policies appear to have cancelled — try to win them back or at least learn why they left.
past_actions.emotional_state: Controlled unease with a surface of confident professionalism. There is a low hum of anxiety underneath — the kind Tom has learned to keep below the level of conscious attention. The sector data number sits somewhere between the back of his mind and his stomach. He does not dwell on it. Dwelling would mean admitting something he isn't ready to admit.

past_actions.summary: Attend Maria Santos's town hall to learn about the $2,500 retraining grants. Go not as someone seeking a grant — go as someone who wants to understand what's happening in the community and what options exist. Sit in the back. Take notes on paper, not on a phone. Do not raise your hand unless the question is purely informational.
past_actions.emotional_state: The controlled professional surface is still there — Tom will not come apart at work, will not let clients see anything except steadiness. But underneath that surface something has quietly shifted. The refrigerator hum stopped. The silence is louder now. He's not scared exactly. He's become the kind of not-scared that is actually the first quiet cousin of scared, the kind that makes you pick up the phone and ask a casual question to your regional manager that isn't casual at all.

past_actions.summary: Participate in Linda Park's one-on-one meeting. Give her honest, specific field intelligence about customer cancellations — the real reasons clients are leaving: they sold their cars, switched to RoboRide, or couldn't justify the premium when they're barely driving. Frame it professionally as data, not despair. In exchange, probe Linda for what AutoShield's regional strategy is: are they pivoting to new product lines, are there internal transfers available, is there a corporate retraining program? Listen more than I talk. Take mental notes on whether she seems like she has a plan or whether she's just gathering data to manage upward.

Respond to Linda Park's briefing on the commercial rideshare and AV liability pivot with a professionally worded acknowledgment. Express willingness to learn about the new product lines. Do not push back, do not ask hard questions about timeline or job security, do not match Priya's energy or ambition. Say the right words. Keep my head down. What I'm actually signaling is: I am not a problem, I am not resistant, I am manageable. This buys time.

reflections.reflection: I have spent six ticks managing appearances instead of managing reality. The tick 5 strategy — say the right words, keep my head down, signal that I am not a problem — cost $2,697 and produced nothing actionable. I have been treating Linda Park's perception of me as the resource worth protecting, when the resource that actually matters is the 17 months of runway left in my savings account. Priya Sharma has been trying to have an honest conversation with me and I have been too busy performing calm professionalism to show up for it. That ends this tick.
reflections.identity_shift: Something is loosening in the attachment to the role of 'experienced, steady insurance professional.' That identity was load-bearing for a long time. It is still there, but I can feel it becoming more of a history than a present-tense fact. I am beginning — slowly, reluctantly — to consider that the 28 years are not a credential that will transfer automatically. They are a foundation I have to consciously build from. That is a different thing.
regrets: Did not apply for the $2,500 retraining grant after the town hall in tick 2. Four ticks of delay for no reason except not wanting to admit I needed it.
Spent ticks 5 performing manageability for Linda Park instead of taking one concrete structural action. The money drained and the position is unchanged.

Did not engage with Priya Sharma honestly when she first signaled she wanted a real conversation. She is the highest-trust colleague I have. I treated her like a threat to manage instead of a resource to think alongside.
successes: The tick 4 one-on-one with Linda Park produced real intelligence — I now know AutoShield is attempting a commercial fleet and AV liability pivot. That information has value even if I haven't used it yet.
I have maintained employment and kept the surface professional enough that I have not been categorized as a problem by management. That buys time, even if it costs money.
reflections.adaptation_notes: The pattern I need to break: mistaking the absence of catastrophe for the presence of a plan. Keeping my head down is a posture, not a strategy. The actual adaptation path requires two things I have been avoiding: (1) engaging Priya as a genuine thought partner on what lateral moves exist in insurance adjacent fields, and (2) treating the retraining grant as real money rather than a symbol of defeat. The math says 17 months at current burn. That is the real constraint. Every action from here gets evaluated against that number.
